--- title: "Distributional assumptions" description: "Most machine-learning models predict without Normal data or equal spread, but the distribution still decides what a prediction means and how sure it can be. A random forest's errors fail both checks; trained on log counts it predicts far fewer animals than were caught, and a quantile forest gives intervals that follow the errors." order: 2 categories: [assumptions] --- ## Normal data and equal spread are not requirements of machine learning Statistics courses teach two checks before a model is fitted: that the model's errors follow a **Normal distribution** (the bell curve), and that their spread is the same everywhere, **equal spread** (homogeneity of variance, in statistics). Counts of animals usually fail both. Most machine-learning models predict without either: trees, forests and boosting split the data by the order of its values, whatever its shape. The exception is the generative model of [Discriminative and generative models](../01-introduction/discriminative-and-generative-models.qmd), which describes the data with a shape. The distribution still matters in two places: what a prediction means, and how sure it can be. This page follows one random forest through both. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Each loss aims at a different middle of the data A prediction is one number standing for all the catches a station could give, and the loss decides which number. [Loss functions](../04-how-algorithms-learn/loss-functions.qmd) set squared error against absolute error. Squared error is smallest at the **average** of the catches, and absolute error at the **median**, the middle catch. A **quantile loss** aims at any chosen point: its 95% version at the catch that only 1 in 20 stations exceed. For a symmetric bell curve the average and the median are the same. For counts with a long right tail they are not: a few large catches pull the average above the typical one. A model fitted with squared error predicts the average, which is what a total needs: predicted animals per station times the number of stations. Any step that changes what the loss aims at changes that total, and the second part of the worked example shows a common one. ::: {.diagram} ![The errors of a model fitted to counts are skewed and spread wider where more is predicted. Squared error on log counts aims at the typical catch, below the average, so totals come out short. A Normal interval has one width and reaches below zero, while intervals from quantiles widen where the catches do.](img/spread.svg){fig-alt="Three cards. Skewed errors, widen as predictions grow: a scatter of points that fans out to the right around a rising line; most models predict well anyway, and the checks say where to take care. Log counts, aim below the average: a histogram with a long right tail, a dashed line at the median marked log counts aim here and a solid line further right at the average marked a total needs this; squared error on log counts aims at the typical catch, so totals come out short. Intervals, follow the errors: the fan-shaped scatter with a dashed band of one width, marked Normal, that reaches below zero on the left, and a blue band from quantiles that starts narrow above zero and widens to the right; a Normal band has one width, and quantiles widen where the catches do. A note says the distribution decides what a prediction means and how sure it can be."} ::: ## Worked example The data, the split by site and the recipe are those of [Forests and boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd), with missing values filled with the median. The training sites are dealt into ten folds for cross-validation by site, as in [Hyperparameter selection](../05-generalisation/hyperparameter-selection.qmd). ### Preparing the data ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() split <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) |> mutate(log_abundance = log(abundance + 1)) test <- testing(split) # ten folds of training sites folds <- group_vfold_cv(train, group = site_id, v = 10) tree_recipe <- recipe( abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate + season, data = train ) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) tibble(stations = nrow(train), empty = sum(train$abundance == 0), median = median(train$abundance), average = round(mean(train$abundance), 1), largest = max(train$abundance)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| stations| empty| median| average| largest| |--------:|-----:|------:|-------:|-------:| | 598| 129| 3| 4| 40|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor, RandomForestRegressor from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold, GroupShuffleSplit, cross_val_predict from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() numeric = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"] categorical = ["substrate", "season"] predictors = numeric + categorical grouper = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) train_rows, test_rows = next(grouper.split(survey, groups=survey["site_id"])) train, test = survey.iloc[train_rows], survey.iloc[test_rows] # ten folds of training sites folds = GroupKFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=123) # scikit-learn's trees need numbers, so the recipe also makes 0/1 columns. tree_recipe = ColumnTransformer([ ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric), ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(sparse_output=False), categorical), ]) def pipeline(model): return Pipeline([("recipe", tree_recipe), ("model", model)]) counts = train["abundance"] pd.DataFrame({"stations": [len(train)], "empty": [(counts == 0).sum()], "median": [counts.median()], "average": [round(counts.mean(), 1)], "largest": [counts.max()]}) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | stations | empty | median | average | largest | |-----------:|--------:|---------:|----------:|----------:| | 575 | 133 | 2 | 3.7 | 37 | ::: ::: ::: The counts are far from a bell curve. 129 of the 598 training stations caught nothing, the median station caught 3 animals and the largest 40, and the long tail lifts the average to 4.0. ### The forest's errors are skewed and widen with its predictions A model's errors are the place to check both assumptions, and they must be errors on sites the model did not see. Cross-validation gives one for every training station: each fold's stations are predicted by a forest fitted to the other nine folds. The forest is that of [Forests and boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd), here with 500 trees, fitted with squared error. The errors are then split into fifths by the size of the prediction. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} forest_model <- rand_forest(mode = "regression", trees = 500) |> set_engine("ranger", seed = 123) forest <- workflow(tree_recipe, forest_model) # every training station, predicted by a forest that never saw its site errors <- fit_resamples(forest, folds, control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE)) |> collect_predictions() |> arrange(.row) |> transmute(caught = abundance, predicted = .pred, error = caught - predicted, fifth = ntile(predicted, 5)) spread <- errors |> summarise(predicted_from = min(predicted), predicted_to = max(predicted), error_sd = sd(error), .by = fifth) |> arrange(fifth) spread |> mutate(across(-fifth, \(x) round(x, 1))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| fifth| predicted_from| predicted_to| error_sd| |-----:|--------------:|------------:|--------:| | 1| 0.2| 2.1| 1.8| | 2| 2.1| 3.4| 3.1| | 3| 3.4| 4.5| 4.6| | 4| 4.5| 5.9| 4.2| | 5| 5.9| 23.8| 7.7|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} forest = pipeline(RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=500, max_features="sqrt", min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=123)) # every training station, predicted by a forest that never saw its site predicted = cross_val_predict(forest, train[predictors], counts, groups=train["site_id"], cv=folds) errors = pd.DataFrame({"caught": counts.to_numpy(), "predicted": predicted}) errors["error"] = errors["caught"] - errors["predicted"] errors["fifth"] = pd.qcut(errors["predicted"].rank(method="first"), 5, labels=False) + 1 spread = (errors.groupby("fifth") .agg(predicted_from=("predicted", "min"), predicted_to=("predicted", "max"), error_sd=("error", "std")) .reset_index()) spread.round(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | fifth | predicted_from | predicted_to | error_sd | |--------:|-----------------:|---------------:|-----------:| | 1 | 0.4 | 2.1 | 1.9 | | 2 | 2.1 | 3.1 | 3.2 | | 3 | 3.1 | 4 | 4.9 | | 4 | 4 | 5.2 | 3.9 | | 5 | 5.2 | 12.4 | 5.5 | ::: ::: ::: @fig-errors shows both checks. The errors are not Normal: 62% of the stations caught fewer animals than predicted, the middle station 0.9 fewer, while a few caught far more, up to 30 above the prediction. The spread is not equal either. In the fifth of stations with the smallest predictions the errors have a standard deviation of 1.8 animals, and in the fifth with the largest, 7.7: 4.3 times as wide. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} middle_90 <- errors |> summarise(from = min(predicted), to = max(predicted), low = quantile(error, 0.05), high = quantile(error, 0.95), .by = fifth) shape_plot <- ggplot(errors, aes(error)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = ml_palette[["blue"]], alpha = 0.7) + geom_function(fun = \(x) nrow(errors) * dnorm(x, mean(errors$error), sd(errors$error)), colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], linewidth = 1) + labs(x = "Error (animals caught − predicted)", y = "Stations", title = "Skewed, not bell-shaped") spread_plot <- ggplot(errors, aes(predicted, error)) + geom_rect(data = middle_90, aes(xmin = from, xmax = to, ymin = low, ymax = high), inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = ml_palette[["blue"]], alpha = 0.15) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey50") + geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 1.2) + labs(x = "Predicted count", y = "Error (animals)", title = "Wider where more is predicted") shape_plot + spread_plot ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The random forest's errors on sites it did not see, one for each training station. Left: their histogram, against a Normal curve with the same mean and spread; the errors bunch below zero and trail far above it. Right: each error against the prediction, with the middle 90% of the errors in each fifth of the predictions shaded; the errors spread wider as the prediction grows.](distributional-assumptions_files/figure-html/fig-errors-1.png){#fig-errors fig-alt='Two panels. Left, a histogram of the errors in animals, with a Normal curve of the same mean and standard deviation drawn over it: the histogram peaks just below zero, where 62% of the errors lie, and has a long tail to the right reaching 30, which the symmetric Normal curve does not follow. Right, the errors against the predicted count, with five shaded boxes, one for each fifth of the predictions, covering the middle 90% of the errors: the box for the smallest predictions is narrow and the boxes grow taller to the right, where the standard deviation reaches 7.7 animals against 1.8 on the left.' width=1700} ::: ::: ::: Neither stops the forest. Its predictions are averages of the catches at similar stations, and an average needs no particular shape and no equal spread. What the shape changes is what a prediction means, and how sure the forest can be. ### Training on log counts predicts far fewer animals than were caught A common recipe for skewed data is to make it more Normal first: fit the model to the log of the count, plus 1 so that empty stations stay at zero, and turn each prediction back with the exponential, minus 1. The second forest does exactly that, and both are scored on the same cross-validated stations: by RMSE, and by the total number of animals they predict across the 598 stations against the total caught. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} log_recipe <- recipe( log_abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate + season, data = train ) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) log_predicted <- fit_resamples(workflow(log_recipe, forest_model), folds, control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE)) |> collect_predictions() |> arrange(.row) |> pull(.pred) errors <- errors |> mutate(log_predicted = exp(log_predicted) - 1) # back to animals totals <- tibble( model = c("Random forest", "Random forest on log counts"), rmse = c(rmse_vec(errors$caught, errors$predicted), rmse_vec(errors$caught, errors$log_predicted)), predicted_total = c(sum(errors$predicted), sum(errors$log_predicted)), caught_total = sum(errors$caught) ) totals |> mutate(rmse = round(rmse, 2), predicted_total = round(predicted_total)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|model | rmse| predicted_total| caught_total| |:---------------------------|----:|---------------:|------------:| |Random forest | 4.69| 2514| 2421| |Random forest on log counts | 4.78| 1699| 2421|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} log_predicted = cross_val_predict(forest, train[predictors], np.log(counts + 1), groups=train["site_id"], cv=folds) errors["log_predicted"] = np.exp(log_predicted) - 1 # back to animals totals = pd.DataFrame({ "model": ["Random forest", "Random forest on log counts"], "rmse": [root_mean_squared_error(errors["caught"], errors[column]) for column in ["predicted", "log_predicted"]], "predicted_total": [errors["predicted"].sum(), errors["log_predicted"].sum()], "caught_total": errors["caught"].sum(), }) totals.round({"rmse": 2, "predicted_total": 0}) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | model | rmse | predicted_total | caught_total | |:----------------------------|-------:|------------------:|---------------:| | Random forest | 4.11 | 2142 | 2128 | | Random forest on log counts | 4.27 | 1445 | 2128 | ::: ::: ::: The two forests score almost the same: an RMSE of 4.69 on raw counts and 4.78 on log counts. Their totals do not. The stations caught 2421 animals; the forest on raw counts predicts 2514, and the forest on log counts 1699, 30% short. @fig-log shows that the shortfall runs through every fifth of the stations, not just the largest. On the log scale, squared error aims at the average log count. Turned back into animals, that is close to the median, the typical catch, and for skewed counts the typical catch sits below the average. The forest on log counts answers a different question, and the RMSE does not show it. A survey that sums its predictions into a stock estimate, a biomass or a map total would come out 30% short with no warning. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} by_fifth |> pivot_longer(-fifth, names_to = "series", values_to = "animals") |> mutate(series = fct_inorder(series)) |> ggplot(aes(fifth, animals, colour = series)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 2.5) + scale_colour_manual(values = c("Caught" = "grey40", "Random forest" = ml_palette[["blue"]], "Random forest on log counts" = ml_palette[["vermilion"]])) + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) + labs(x = "Fifth of the stations, by the forest's prediction", y = "Animals per station", colour = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The average catch per station in each fifth of the forest's predictions, against the average each forest predicts there. The forest on raw counts follows the catch; the forest on log counts falls short in every fifth.](distributional-assumptions_files/figure-html/fig-log-1.png){#fig-log fig-alt='Points joined by lines for five groups of training stations, ordered by the forest prediction, with the average animals per station on the vertical axis. The caught averages, in grey, rise from 1.4 to 7.2. The forest on raw counts, in blue, lies close to them. The forest on log counts, in vermilion, lies below them in every group, from 0.8 to 5.5.' width=1400} ::: ::: ::: Keep the counts as they are when the totals matter. For a skewed outcome, a loss built for it, such as the Poisson deviance of [Loss functions](../04-how-algorithms-learn/loss-functions.qmd), changes the weights without changing what the prediction aims at. ### A quantile forest gives intervals that follow the errors A prediction says how many animals to expect. A **prediction interval** says how far the catch may land from it: a 90% interval should contain 9 catches in 10. The textbook interval makes both assumptions: it is symmetric, as a bell curve is, and it has one width, 1.64 standard deviations of the errors either side of every prediction. A **quantile forest** makes neither. It grows the same trees as the forest, but keeps every training catch in each leaf instead of only their average, and reads the 5% and 95% points off the catches that land with a new station. Both intervals are built from a forest fitted on all the training stations, and checked on the test sites. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} half_width <- qnorm(0.95) * sd(errors$error) # 1.64 standard deviations quantile_fit <- workflow( tree_recipe, rand_forest(mode = "regression", trees = 500) |> set_engine("ranger", seed = 123, quantreg = TRUE) ) |> fit(train) # ranger reads the quantiles off the recipe's output ends <- predict(extract_fit_engine(quantile_fit), bake(extract_recipe(quantile_fit), new_data = test), type = "quantiles", quantiles = c(0.05, 0.95))$predictions covered <- tibble(predicted = predict(quantile_fit, test)$.pred, caught = test$abundance) |> mutate(fifth = ntile(predicted, 5), order = rank(predicted, ties.method = "first")) intervals <- bind_rows( "Normal" = mutate(covered, low = predicted - half_width, high = predicted + half_width), "Quantile forest" = mutate(covered, low = ends[, 1], high = ends[, 2]), .id = "interval" ) |> mutate(inside = caught >= low & caught <= high) intervals |> summarise(inside = mean(inside), width = mean(high - low), below_zero = mean(low < 0), .by = c(interval, fifth)) |> arrange(interval, fifth) |> mutate(across(c(inside, width, below_zero), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|interval | fifth| inside| width| below_zero| |:---------------|-----:|------:|-----:|----------:| |Normal | 1| 1.00| 15.43| 1.00| |Normal | 2| 0.95| 15.43| 1.00| |Normal | 3| 1.00| 15.43| 1.00| |Normal | 4| 0.88| 15.43| 1.00| |Normal | 5| 0.90| 15.43| 0.85| |Quantile forest | 1| 0.95| 5.12| 0.00| |Quantile forest | 2| 0.90| 8.35| 0.00| |Quantile forest | 3| 0.98| 11.44| 0.00| |Quantile forest | 4| 0.92| 12.99| 0.00| |Quantile forest | 5| 1.00| 18.31| 0.00|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} from scipy.stats import norm half_width = norm.ppf(0.95) * errors["error"].std() # 1.64 standard deviations forest_fit = forest.fit(train[predictors], counts) covered = pd.DataFrame({"predicted": forest_fit.predict(test[predictors]), "caught": test["abundance"].to_numpy()}) covered["fifth"] = pd.qcut(covered["predicted"].rank(method="first"), 5, labels=False) + 1 # scikit-learn has no quantile forest, so boosting with a quantile loss gives # the two ends, one model for each. def end(quantile): model = pipeline(HistGradientBoostingRegressor( loss="quantile", quantile=quantile, random_state=123)) fitted = model.fit(train[predictors], counts) return fitted.predict(test[predictors]) intervals = pd.concat({ "Normal": covered.assign(low=covered["predicted"] - half_width, high=covered["predicted"] + half_width), "Quantile boosting": covered.assign(low=end(0.05), high=end(0.95)), }, names=["interval"]).reset_index(level="interval") intervals["inside"] = intervals["caught"].between(intervals["low"], intervals["high"]) (intervals .assign(width=intervals["high"] - intervals["low"], below_zero=intervals["low"] < 0) .groupby(["interval", "fifth"]) .agg(inside=("inside", "mean"), width=("width", "mean"), below_zero=("below_zero", "mean")) .reset_index().round(2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | interval | fifth | inside | width | below_zero | |:------------------|--------:|---------:|--------:|-------------:| | Normal | 1 | 1 | 13.54 | 1 | | Normal | 2 | 0.98 | 13.54 | 1 | | Normal | 3 | 0.93 | 13.54 | 1 | | Normal | 4 | 0.96 | 13.54 | 1 | | Normal | 5 | 0.69 | 13.54 | 0.73 | | Quantile boosting | 1 | 0.93 | 3.81 | 0 | | Quantile boosting | 2 | 0.89 | 5.95 | 0 | | Quantile boosting | 3 | 0.89 | 8.24 | 0 | | Quantile boosting | 4 | 0.87 | 10.04 | 0 | | Quantile boosting | 5 | 0.78 | 12.93 | 0 | ::: ::: ::: The Normal interval runs 7.7 animals either side of every prediction and holds 95% of the test catches, against the 90% it promises. Both assumptions show in where it goes wrong (@fig-intervals). It is symmetric, but the errors are not: for 97% of the stations its lower end is below zero, a catch no survey can make, and 9 of the 11 catches outside it lie above it. It has one width, but the spread does not: where the forest predicts least it is 15 animals wide, though 76% of the catches there were 0 or 1. The quantile forest's intervals never reach below zero. They widen from 5.1 animals in the fifth with the smallest predictions to 18.3 in the fifth with the largest, and hold between 90% and 100% of the catches in every fifth. They are a little wider than they need to be, but they are wide in the right places. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(intervals, aes(order)) + annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = -Inf, ymax = 0, fill = "grey85") + geom_linerange(aes(ymin = low, ymax = high), colour = ml_palette[["blue"]], alpha = 0.5, linewidth = 0.6) + geom_point(aes(y = caught, colour = inside), size = 1.2) + facet_wrap(~interval) + scale_colour_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "grey40", "FALSE" = ml_palette[["vermilion"]]), labels = c("TRUE" = "Inside", "FALSE" = "Outside")) + labs(x = "Test stations, from the smallest prediction to the largest", y = "Animals caught", colour = "Catch") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The 90% prediction intervals for the test stations, ordered by the forest's prediction. Left: the Normal interval, one width everywhere, reaching below zero wherever little is predicted. Right: the quantile forest's, narrow and above zero where little is predicted, widening where more is. Catches outside their interval are in vermilion.](distributional-assumptions_files/figure-html/fig-intervals-1.png){#fig-intervals fig-alt='Two panels, one for each kind of interval, each showing every test station as a vertical line from its interval low end to its high end, in order of its forest prediction from left to right, with the caught count as a point; a shaded strip marks values below zero. Left, the Normal interval: every line is 15 animals long, and for 97% of the stations it reaches into the shaded strip; 11 catches lie outside, 9 of them above. Right, the quantile forest: the lines start short and above zero at small predictions and grow longer to the right, from about 5.1 to 18.3 animals; 10 catches lie outside.' width=1700} ::: ::: ::: For a statistical model the same assumptions set its confidence intervals: [Count regression](../03-supervised-learning/count-regression.qmd) found Poisson regression's too narrow for counts this spread out. Every check on this page also treats the stations as independent, which [Independence of observations](independence-of-observations.qmd) tests. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - Most machine-learning models predict without Normal data or equal spread. The distribution still decides what a prediction means and how sure it can be. - Squared error aims at the **average**, absolute error at the **median**, and a **quantile loss** at any chosen point. For skewed counts they differ. - The random forest's errors on unseen sites were skewed, and 4.3 times as spread out at the largest predictions as at the smallest. Its predictions did not need either assumption. - Trained on log counts, the forest scored about the same RMSE but predicted 30% fewer animals than were caught: it aimed at the typical catch, not the average. - A Normal **prediction interval** reached below zero for 97% of the test stations and missed mostly large catches. A **quantile forest** gave intervals that widened where the catches did. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Fit the forest on log counts to all the training stations and predict the test sites. Ask the quantile forest for its 50% point, the median, at the same stations. How close are the two? 2. Fit the boosted model of [Forests and boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd) to the raw counts with Poisson deviance, `set_engine("xgboost", objective = "count:poisson")`, and compare its total with the forest's.
